food.text: From c. 1650 BC, elaborately decorated bronze vessels were placed in the tombs of royalty and nobility during the Chinese Bronze Age. They were made so that an individual or a social group could offer food and drink to ancestors and other deities or spirits.

Documented excavations have found over 200 ritual bronze pieces in a single royal tomb. The vessels held offerings of food and drink for ancestors and spirits, so royal burials could contain a huge banqueting set.
Shang settlement was centered on river valleys, driven in part by the introduction of intensive agriculture. Farming helped shape where the bronze-casting Shang civilisation lived.
Evidence suggests cattle husbandry reached China only in the late Neolithic, around 3600 to 2000 BCE. The earliest examples of cattle come from the regions of Gansu and Qinghai.
When the owner of a ritual bronze died, it was often placed in his tomb so that he could continue to pay his respects in the afterlife. Other examples were cast specifically as grave goods.

The ritual bronzes were likely not used for normal eating and drinking. They were larger, more elaborate versions of everyday vessels, made in precious materials, and many of the shapes also survive in pottery.

In a band of highlands stretching from the edge of the Tibetan plateau through the Ordos Plateau to the northeast, cultures shifted in the early second millennium BC from an agricultural economy to a mixed agropastoral or fully pastoral one. These cultures linked the plains with the Eurasian steppe.

Shang oracle bones contain the first surviving Chinese characters. Many bronze vessels from the Shang dynasty were apparently used to warm alcohol, and millet was the area's staple grain, so the drinks may have resembled modern huangjiu. Some of the common alloys used to cast such bronze vessels held up to 20% free lead, so it is an open question to what extent ancient elites may have been poisoning themselves.

art.text: From about 1650 BC, elaborately decorated bronze vessels were placed in the tombs of royalty and nobility in China. Excavations have found over 200 pieces in a single royal tomb. Many were buried so that the owner could keep paying respects to ancestors in the afterlife.

The Chinese Bronze Age began in the Xia dynasty, around 2070 to 1600 BC. Bronze ritual vessels reached their peak in the Shang dynasty, and they were so important that the Imperial art collections gave them an entire separate catalogue.

Painted pottery in Neolithic China can be traced back to the Yangshao and Longshan cultures of the Yellow River valley. During the Bronze Age, artisans of the Shang and Zhou dynasties then produced multitudes of artistic bronze vessels. These served practical purposes, but also religious ritual and geomancy.

Ritual bronzes were made for offering food and drink to ancestors and other deities or spirits. The ceremonies, held in family temples or halls over tombs, can be seen as ritual banquets in which both living and dead members of a family were supposed to take part.

The guang was a Shang dynasty ewer for pouring rice wine at ritual banquets. It has a single thick foot and a hollow body representing stylized animals, with an animal-shaped handle at one end and a spout at the other. Many were richly decorated with taotie.

Jade was called yu by 3000 BC, and it has been prominent in Chinese art since prehistoric times. An important early jade form was the circular disk known as bi, generally understood to represent the heavens in some fashion.

The Liangzhu culture of the 3rd millennium BCE is where the Six Ritual Jades are found: the bi, the cong, the huang, the hu, the gui, and the zhang. Their meanings were not mentioned before the eastern Zhou dynasty. By the time of the Rites of Zhou they were thought to represent the sky, the earth, and the four directions.

Ritual bronzes were likely not used for everyday eating and drinking. They were larger, more elaborate versions of ordinary vessels, which were made in precious materials. Many shapes also survive in pottery, and pottery versions continued to be made in an antiquarian spirit until modern times.

Guang vessels served wine at ancestor worship rituals. The wine vapors were meant to be consumed by the deceased spirits, while the actual contents were enjoyed by the living. Guangs were also sometimes placed in the grave of the deceased.
The earliest metal bells in China date to about 2000 BC, with one found at the Taosi site and four at the Erlitou site. They may have been derived from an earlier pottery prototype.

According to Robert Bagley, the lid is the chief characteristic of the guang, because it is where the largest relief and decoration often appear. Yet the animal and fantastic creature ornament has no exactly known purpose, and its meaning is still left to interpretation.

war.text: Chinese war chariots appear in the archaeological record from around 1200 BCE, during the Late Shang period, where they were used on open fields and plains. They were probably introduced through the northern steppes, probably from the area of the Deer stones culture.

Shang oracle bone inscriptions were used for divinations on behalf of the king. They record royal concerns such as weather and the harvest, and also warfare with neighbouring polities and the mobilizing of workers for warfare. Campaigns and raids also supplied captives to be sacrificed in Shang rituals, and the inscriptions record numbers of enemies killed or captured and booty taken.

Most surviving ancient Chinese bronzes are ritual forms rather than versions made for practical use as tools or weapons. Weapons like daggers and axes had a sacrificial meaning, symbolizing the heavenly power of the ruler.

The Erligang city at Zhengzhou was surrounded by a roughly rectangular rammed-earth wall with a perimeter of about 7 kilometers. The walls would have been about 20 meters wide at the base and rose to a height of 8 meters. Large workshops stood outside the walls, including a bone workshop, a pottery workshop and two bronze vessel workshops.

Traditional sources credit the invention of the chariot to Xi Zhong, a minister of the Xia dynasty, and say chariots were used at the Battle of Gan in the 21st century BCE. Archaeological evidence, however, shows only small scale use beginning around 1200 BCE in the Late Shang period.
The Late Shang capital site near Anyang had no city wall. A canal or moat around the central district became blocked in the later reigns, which suggests the Shang felt no danger of invasion.
Chariots gave military commanders a mobile platform from which to control troops. They also gave archers and soldiers armed with dagger-axes increased mobility on the battlefield.

The earth walls of Zhengzhou, built in the 15th century BC, were 20 metres wide at the base and 8 metres high, running about 7 kilometres around the city. Rammed earth fortification was an inherited tradition, since much older walls have been found at Longshan culture sites from about 3000 to 2000 BC.

The Tomb of Fu Hao, thought to belong to a consort of Wu Ding, was found intact. It held 16 human victims and a dog, along with 1,600 kg (3,500 lb) of bronze vessels, weapons and tools, 755 jades, 110 pieces of worked stone, 564 objects of carved bone, two ivory cups inlaid with turquoise, 6,880 cowrie shells and 11 pots. Fu Hao was a military leader known from the oracle bone inscriptions, and several of them mention troops raised and led by her.

Chariot commanders carried a bronze dagger in case the chariot became unserviceable or an enemy jumped on board. Soldiers aboard wore leather or occasionally copper armour and carried a shield made from leather or bronze.

literature.text: Most Shang writing takes the form of inscriptions on oracle bones used for divinations for the king. The inscriptions reveal royal concerns such as weather, the harvest, warfare, and mobilizing workers for warfare or agricultural work.

Late Shang oracle bone inscriptions are the oldest known form of Chinese writing. They are the ancestor of modern Chinese characters. Because they survive, the Late Shang can be confirmed as a historical state.
The Late Shang is the earliest known literate civilization in China. It began with King Wu Ding in the second half of the 13th century BC. Its capital was at a site near Anyang now known as Yinxu.

The Erlitou and Erligang cultures of the Yellow River valley were Bronze Age civilizations that came before the historical record. Written history in China first emerges around 1250 BCE at Yinxu, during the Late Shang.

Most Shang writing is inscribed on oracle bones used for divinations on behalf of the king. Shang ritual centred on offerings to ancestors, which included animal and human victims killed in sacrifice, and the inscriptions record them. From these records modern investigators can deduce a king list that largely matches the one in Sima Qian's histories and the Bamboo Annals.

The oracle bone inscriptions reveal the concerns of Shang kings. They record worries about the weather and the harvest, warfare with neighbouring polities, and the mobilizing of workers for warfare or agricultural work.

The Tomb of Fu Hao at Yinxu was one of the richest finds from the Late Shang. It is thought to belong to a consort of Wu Ding who is mentioned in Shang inscriptions. The medium-sized tomb held 16 human victims and a dog, along with 1,600 kg of bronze, 755 jades and 6,880 cowrie shells.

The oracle bone script is an early form of Chinese characters. It says little about the sounds of the language. Still, characters borrowed to write different words fit current theories about Western Zhou Chinese.

Several Shang dynasty oracle bone inscriptions record the hunting of the sì, a creature that may be a rhinoceros or a wild buffalo. One famous inscription tells how an accident befell King Wu Ding's hunting party in pursuit of a sì: the carriage of courtier Chu broke its axis, a gelding tripped over stones and bolted away from the king's carriage, and Prince Yang also fell down.

Later historians such as Sima Qian describe a Xia dynasty (c. 2070 to c. 1600 BC). No writing has been excavated at Erlitou or any other contemporaneous site, so there is not enough evidence to prove whether the Xia ever existed.

Traditional accounts such as Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian tell legends about how alcohol began. One says the brewer Yidi presented the first alcoholic beverage as a gift to the emperor Yu the Great around 2100 BC. Another credits Du Kang with inventing it.

science.text: Chinese star names that were later grouped into the twenty-eight mansions have been found on oracle bones unearthed at Anyang, dating to the mid-Shang dynasty. This shows that the ancient Chinese were identifying stars from 1300 BCE.

The earliest metal objects in China date to around 2,900 BC, and most early finds come from the northwest, mainly Gansu and Qinghai. Metallurgy there grew into established centers of copper and bronze production by the late third millennium BC.

The core of the Chinese "mansion" (xiù) system of star groupings also took shape around the time of King Wu Ding (1250-1192 BCE). It became a basis for Chinese astronomy, which centered on close observation of circumpolar stars.

A knife from the Majiayao culture found at Linjia, Gansu, dated to between 2900 and 2740 BC, is the earliest copper alloy artifact of secure stratigraphic provenience from China. However, a 2016 journal article concluded from isotopes, the lack of nearby ore deposits and the lack of a smelting site that it was most likely imported.

By 1500 BC, excellent bronzes were being made in China in large quantities, partly as a display of status. As many as 200 large pieces were buried with their owner for use in the afterlife, as in the Tomb of Fu Hao, a Shang queen.

Socketed spearheads with a single side hook appear in China around 2100–2000 BCE, during the Taosi culture, in the earliest and most faithful Seima-Turbino types. This suggests Chinese bronze metallurgy initially derived from the Eurasian steppes. China then refined the technology through its mastery of bronze casting.

Ritual bronzes from the Shang and Zhou dynasties all depicted elephants with two 'fingers' on the tip of the trunk, whereas the Indian elephant has only one. A 2011 study by scientists from China used this to argue that the ancient elephants of China were probably of the genus Palaeoloxodon.

Shang astronomers invented a sophisticated calendar based on a 60-day cycle. It was used to schedule the ceremonies through which royal adherents constantly worshipped their deities. Religion thus shaped how the Shang organized time itself.

Early China used two bronze smelting techniques, the section mold process and the lost-wax process. The bronze knife from Majiayao at Linjia, dated to about 3000 BC, was made by the section mold process, in which two molds are spliced together.

From around 2000 BC, cast bronze objects such as the socketed spear with a single side hook were imported into China and adapted from the Seima-Turbino culture. Early Chinese bronze technology thus drew on outside influences.

A bronze hatchet with a blade of meteoric iron was excavated near the city of Gaocheng in Shijiazhuang, now in Hebei. It has been dated to the 14th century BC, combining bronze with iron from a meteorite.

Some of the earliest Chinese bronze mirrors belonged to the late Neolithic Qijia culture from around 2000 BCE. Even so, until Warring States times bronze mirrors were not common, with only about twenty discovered.

Late Shang dynasty artifacts, including socketed spearheads with a single side hook and knives with deer-headed pommels, resemble Seima-Turbino ones. Some come from the tomb of Fu Hao, who died c. 1200 BCE. They may reflect a century-long conflict between the Shang and the northern Guifang, which possibly transferred objects and techniques.

Fossil elephant experts Victoria Herridge and Adrian Lister disagree with the claim that China's ancient elephants were Palaeoloxodon. They say the supposed dental features are contrast artifacts caused by the low resolution of the figures in the scientific paper, and are not visible in better photographs.
In 2008, two iron fragments were excavated at the Mogou site in Gansu and dated to the 14th century BC, in the period of the Siwa culture. One was made of bloomery iron rather than meteoritic iron.

A recent compositional analysis proposed that the metals used for Chinese ritual bronzes came from mining progressively deeper ores in deposits close to where many of the bronzes were unearthed. This questions the idea that Bronze Age China acquired its metals from distant regions.

politics.text: Whether the Xia dynasty existed is still debated, because no writing has been excavated at Erlitou or any other contemporaneous site. Many Chinese archaeologists link the Xia to the Erlitou culture, whose site has the earliest evidence of an elite performing rituals with cast bronze vessels.

The Shang dynasty is the earliest Chinese dynasty firmly supported by archaeological evidence. Excavations at Yinxu, near modern Anyang and the final Shang capital of Yin, revealed eleven major royal tombs and palace foundations, along with the remains of humans and animals sacrificed in official state rituals. The Shang practised human sacrifice alongside war: most victims named in Shang writings were war captives taken from the Qiang people to the northwest, and isotope analysis of sacrificial victims at Zhengzhou found they were most likely war captives too. In royal burials, hundreds of commoners, who may have been slaves, were buried alive with the royal corpse.

Before the Xia, Chinese tradition described a notion called gong tianxia, meaning 'All under Heaven belongs to the public', in which leadership passed by abdication rather than inheritance. Under the Xia this gave way to jia tianxia, 'All under Heaven belongs to the ruling family'.

Jie, the last king of Xia, was said to be immoral, lascivious and tyrannical, as with many last rulers in Chinese historiography. He was overthrown by Tang, who founded the Shang dynasty. Tang is said to have given the remnants of the Xia clan the small state of Qi as a fief, a practice called 'the two crownings and the three respects'.

Human sacrifice was a significant part of Shang politics and religion. A saying found in places of religion and politics declared 'The great national concerns are sacrifice and war', which historian Xinxu Liu calls a 'status symbol for rulers'. According to historian Keren Wang, the Shang king would demonstrate devotion to the supreme deity through the spectacular spilling of sacrificial human blood, a spectacle staged for those high in power and influence.
politics.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

politics.text: In 1996 the Chinese government commissioned the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, which proposed that the Xia existed between 2070 and 1600 BC. Other estimates differ widely: the traditional chronology of Liu Xin says 2205 to 1766 BC, and the Bamboo Annals gives 1989 to 1558 BC.

At Yinxu, archaeologists found the earliest known Chinese writing, mostly divination texts inscribed on oracle bones such as turtle shells or ox scapulae. More than 20,000 oracle bones were discovered during the initial scientific excavations in the 1920s and 1930s.

The tomb of Fu Hao, an unusually powerful Shang queen, held over two hundred ritual vessels. A contemporary nobleman's tomb contained only twenty-four. Her higher status was meant to be clear to her contemporaries and also, it was believed, to her ancestors and other spirits.

philosophy.text: Long before the Shang kings, people in Neolithic and early Bronze Age China already showed the beliefs that later marked Shang religion. Animism, ancestor veneration and pyromancy, the practice of burning animal bones to read the cracks, were all present. The early Bronze Age also left abundant evidence of human sacrificial rituals. Ancestor worship in particular survived to influence modern Chinese life.

The Shang state religion (c. 1600 to c. 1046 BC) relied on trained practitioners who communicated with deities, including deceased ancestors and nature spirits. These deities formed a pantheon headed by the high god Di. Communication happened through divinations written on oracle bones and through the sacrifice of living beings, including human beings, in a practice carried out with a certain degree of ritual violence.
Despite its many kinds of spirits, Shang religion was dominated by ancestor worship. Its core beliefs centred on the relationships between the living and the dead.

The earliest attested inscriptions on oracle bones date to c. 1250 BC, during the reign of king Wu Ding. Yet the script was already fully mature, and is believed to have emerged centuries earlier. Much of what we know of Shang religion comes from Yinxu, the Late Shang capital.

The Shang royal lineage regarded itself as divine. Its progenitors were called "sons of God", born by women who "stepped on the imprinting" of Di. The royal ancestors of the early Zhou dynasty were described in the same way.

Shang ritual centred on offerings to ancestors, and those offerings included large numbers of animal and human victims. The oracle bones refer to at least 14,197 human sacrificial victims, including 7,426 Qiang, killed anywhere from 3 to 300 at a time but most commonly 5 to 10. Archaeologists found pits in the temple-palace district holding their skeletons, many decapitated and otherwise mutilated. Because the sacrifices were recorded by ancestor, modern investigators could deduce a king list that largely matches the traditional histories of Sima Qian and the Bamboo Annals.

Traditional texts say Qi, the second king of the Xia dynasty, was a spirit-medium who communicated with Shangdi and sacrificed to the deceased. Although these early periods are often considered mythical, the site of Erlitou shows bronze-using religious activities. These included using scapulae for divination, which the Shang later adopted.

The taotie was a mask-like motif with raised eyes and typically no lower jaw, found on Shang ritual bronze dings. The Lüshi Chunqiu says it has a head but no body, and that when it eats people it does not swallow them but harms them; Sarah Allan reads it as a creature that devoured a man but was damaged in its own body before it could swallow him. Scholar Li Zehou argued that its meaning is not "eating people" but a mysterious communication between people and Heaven (gods), though he held that the idea of it eating people fits its cruel, fearful face, which symbolized fear and force to alien clans and protection to its own.

Scholars disagree over whether Shang religion was bureaucratic or at least proto-bureaucratic. Sinologist Keightley supports such theories, while Eno rejects them. The debate concerns how the Shang pantheon, led by a supreme being, was organized.

Recent investigation found a lack of convincing evidence for shamanism in Shang religion. The shamanic theory of Chang et al. relied on data from later Zhou religious practice, which had been conflated with that of the Shang.

culture.text: Erligang was the first archaeological culture in China to show widespread use of bronze vessel casting. Its bronze vessels became much more widely used and uniform in style than those of the earlier Erlitou culture. The culture existed from approximately 1600 to 1400 BC.

Qijia culture, centered around Lanzhou in Gansu and eastern Qinghai, is regarded as one of the earliest bronze cultures in China. It was distinguished by numerous domesticated horses and by the practice of oracle divination. Its people also produced some of the earliest bronze and copper mirrors found in China.

The Erlitou culture is the earliest large-scale bronze producing culture in China, using a section-mold process to make ritual vessels. The earliest bronze ding in China were found in its fourth stage and were decorated with striped grid patterns. Many archetypal Chinese artifacts were first found at Erlitou sites.

Certain traits of Shang religion, such as animism, ancestor veneration and pyromancy (burning animal bones and interpreting the cracks), are found in the Neolithic and Bronze Age before it. Abundant evidence for human sacrificial rituals also appears in China's early Bronze Age. Ancestor worship was among the prehistoric traditions that influenced modern Chinese life. Studying these religions is hard because there are no contemporary written records.

At Niuheliang, excavators found an underground temple complex with an altar, built of stone platforms with painted walls. Archaeologists named it the Goddess Temple after a clay female head with jade inlaid eyes. Clay figurines as large as three times life size were housed inside.

Human sacrifice was a significant part of ancient Chinese culture, especially under the Shang dynasty, which lasted from about 1600 BC to 1046 BC. The Shang king would show devotion to the supreme deity through the spilling of sacrificial human blood. A phrase from the time held that the great national concerns are sacrifice and war.
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

culture.text: The Qijia cemetery at Mogou in Lintan County, Gansu, has been excavated since 2008, and more than one thousand graves have been found there. Thousands of funerary goods were recovered, including pottery vessels, bone ornaments and implements, shells and metal objects. The graves at Mogou revealed a high level of violence in Qijia culture, and human sacrifice in Qijia culture has also been documented.

Chinese archaeologist Guo Dashun believes the Hongshan culture had a mature system of ancestral worship, which remained important throughout all of Chinese history. Hongshan is believed to have influenced the development of early Chinese civilization.

Jade was worked into ritual objects at Erlitou sites, including ceremonial blades called zhang and ritual dagger-axes called ge. The first bronze ge appeared at Erlitou, where two were found among over 200 bronze artifacts as of 2002. Three jade ge were also discovered at the same site.

The Houmuwu ding is an example of an ancient Chinese bronze used for sacrificial purposes. Its rectangular body is marked with taotie designs. Ancient Chinese bronzes are celebrated for their artistic value and the casting technology used to make them.
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture
